findings.title: RemoteSession can turn an arbitrary namespace Secret into outbound Git credentials
findings.what: Both gitCredentialRef and repo accept unrestricted strings. The only stated repository-host enforcement occurs in the separate server-side dispatch path, so a principal allowed to create RemoteSession objects directly can bypass it, name an otherwise unreadable Secret, and cause its token to be used for a clone to an attacker-controlled host. This converts RemoteSession creation permission into a Secret-exfiltration primitive.
findings.fix: Enforce an HTTPS GitHub-host allowlist and an approved Secret-name policy at Kubernetes admission time, preferably with CRD CEL validations or a validating webhook; do not rely solely on the dispatch server. Bind credential references to explicitly authorized repositories.
findings.acceptance: A direct Kubernetes API request creating a RemoteSession with repo=https://attacker.example/repo and a populated gitCredentialRef is rejected before reconciliation, while an approved GitHub repository and approved credential reference are accepted.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarial re-read confirmed the CRD has no pattern, enum, CEL rule, or webhook enforcing either field. The smallest related baseline controller check confirmed that it mounts the named Secret and constructs the authenticated clone URL from these CR fields; shell quoting prevents command injection but does not prevent credential egress.

findings.title: DashboardInstance permits arbitrary code to run under the managed dashboard identity
findings.what: The image field accepts any string without an allowlist or digest constraint. A principal granted permission to create or update DashboardInstance objects can therefore select an attacker-controlled container image for the operator-managed Deployment, inheriting the managed pod's service-account identity and mounted credentials.
findings.fix: Remove per-CR image selection or enforce an admission-time allowlist of trusted registries/repositories and immutable digests. Use a minimally privileged service account for the resulting workload regardless.
findings.acceptance: The Kubernetes API rejects a DashboardInstance whose image is attacker.example/image:tag or any non-approved, non-digest reference, while accepting the approved digest-pinned dashboard image.
findings.verifyNote: The cited schema was re-read and contains only type:string. The smallest related baseline controller check confirmed that the reconciler copies this value directly into the managed Deployment rather than validating or replacing it.

findings.title: Release workloads default to mutable container tags
findings.what: The session image, dashboard image, and operator manager image all default to or deploy :latest. Registry tag movement can therefore change privileged release workloads without a reviewed manifest change, preventing reproducible rollback and weakening supply-chain integrity.
findings.fix: Pin each release image by immutable sha256 digest, optionally retaining a human-readable version tag alongside the digest, and update those pins only through the reviewed release process.
findings.acceptance: Rendered release manifests and operator defaults contain no :latest references for the manager, dispatch, or dashboard workloads, and every selected image resolves through an explicit sha256 digest.
findings.verifyNote: A separate second pass re-read all three exact references at the immutable baseline. Each remains an active default or active Kustomize image rewrite; none is a commented example or overridden digest in the audited files.
